A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RDLM research work. Their text, equations, tables, figures and Appendices A–D are readable and can be matched despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original RDLM results on Text8, LM1B, CIFAR-10 and promoter DNA, alongside objective and dimension-splitting ablations, transition-distribution simulations and generated samples.

after.justification: v2 retains original results on all four benchmarks, updates several scores and reports the ablations, transition-distribution simulations and generated samples.

M1.justification: The core hypersphere diffusion, mixture paths, Riemannian-normal approximation and dimension splitting remain. The written importance-sampling loss changes from weighting by q(t) in v1 Eq. (20) to 1/q(t) in v2 Eq. (16), also used in Algorithm 1. This is a localized objective correction; the PDFs do not establish whether the implementation changed.

E1.justification: Both evaluate character-level Text8, LM1B language modeling, order-agnostic CIFAR-10 pixel modeling and transcription-conditioned promoter DNA generation. The appendix simulations retain dimensions 4, 256 and 30522. No additional evaluated dataset, domain or task scenario appears.

E2.justification: v2 removes the IAF/SCF comparison row from Text8 Table 1, although its prose still mentions the method. CIFAR-10 Table 3 adds the tau-LDR Absorb comparator alongside the retained tau-LDR row. The LM1B and DNA comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: CIFAR-10 Table 3 changes RDLM's reported size from 35M to 28M parameters. However, v2 Appendix B.3 still specifies 35M, leaving the actual configuration unresolved. The stated dataset splits, sequence lengths and training budgets otherwise remain; the new ten-million-iteration extrapolation does not represent an increased training budget.

E4.justification: The objective and dimension-splitting ablations and MMD approximation analysis are retained. v2 Appendix B.2 adds a brief convergence analysis using a curve-fit extrapolation of validation perplexity, predicting that RDLM surpasses MDLM after ten million iterations. It explicitly states that training stopped at one million iterations.

E5.justification: v2 newly documents Monte Carlo estimation of the negative ELBO using simulated bridge states and reports a curve-fitting extrapolation (Appendices B.1–B.2). These add statistical estimation information, without establishing additional runs. Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals or significance tests; the extrapolation also lacks uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: RDLM's reported LM1B perplexity bound changes from 29.72 to 28.44. CIFAR-10 BPD changes from 2.74 to 2.73, accompanied by inconsistent model-size reporting, so this is not an established same-setting gain. Objective-ablation BPC values change from 1.40/1.39 to 1.36/1.34, and dimension-splitting NLL from 434.2 to 428.5. Main Text8 BPC remains 1.32 and DNA MSE remains 0.027.

T1.justification: v2 Appendix A.5 replaces v1 A.4's simple time-dependent mixture formulation with Proposition A.9 and a Poisson/Fokker–Planck construction containing additional drift terms and explicit regularity assumptions. Appendix A.7 adds a mathematical argument connecting cross-entropy to drift loss and likelihood. Appendix A.2 also restricts interpolation endpoints and removes v1's reverse-flow lemma. These substantially revise the mathematical support.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: connecting discrete diffusion to continuous manifold flows, constructing RDLM, enabling simulation-free training and handling large vocabularies through dimension splitting. The broad performance and multimodal-applicability claims remain substantively the same.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands explanations and qualifications of the retained findings. Appendix B.2 attributes the LM1B gap to untuned hyperparameters, absence of low-discrepancy sampling and incomplete convergence. Section 6.2 attributes image performance to continuous refinement. Appendix D adds a model-capacity explanation for the autoregressive performance gap and proposes a blockwise remedy for the previously stated maximum-length constraint, replacing much of v1's future-directions discussion.

D1.justification: Algorithms 1–3 operationalize existing equations for training, geodesic random-walk sampling and parameter precomputation. Appendix B.1 newly specifies simulated-bridge likelihood evaluation and RTX A5000/H100 hardware; B.2 discloses the lack of hyperparameter search and low-discrepancy sampling. Most dataset-specific implementation details and the code-access link are retained.

R1.justification: The new Appendix A.10 substantially expands comparative positioning: it discusses guidance, design and sampling advantages over discrete diffusion, and distinguishes RDLM from manifold flow matching through its diffusion connection, objectives and scalability. New references cover diffusion solvers, noise scheduling, design choices and multimodal generation. The graph-generation and molecule-synthesis references associated with v1's future directions are removed.

P1.justification: The main exposition is extensively rewritten and reorganized. Simulation-free training moves from a standalone section into Section 3.3, parameterization precedes the likelihood discussion, and background mixture material is consolidated in the appendix. Appendix sections are reorganized, comparison and implementation subsections are added, and Future Directions becomes Limitations and Broader Impacts.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from two-column to predominantly single-column layout, with substantially rearranged tables and equations. v2 adds a conceptual illustration of reparameterization and diffusion paths and three algorithm displays. The existing ablation displays become Tables 5–6, while the retained MMD plots move from Figure 3 to Figure 2.

improvement.justification: The corrected importance weight, expanded derivations, explicit algorithms and evaluation details make the method easier to inspect and reproduce. The additional limitations and comparison discussion also improve context. These gains are tempered by the new CIFAR-10 28M/35M inconsistency and the longer-training superiority claim based on an extrapolation whose fit and uncertainty are not documented.
